name: Tara Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for agreeing to this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Nothing you say will carry your name. Could you walk me through a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a claims assistant at Tailwise, a pet insurer, in a converted warehouse with dogs allowed on Fridays. All day it's vet invoices: a spaniel that ate a sock, a cat with kidney trouble, a rabbit's dental work. I check the treatment is covered, check it isn't a condition the pet had before the policy started, and pay or query it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the animals, obviously, and I like that I can get a worried owner paid in a day. I use AI all day, I've got it reading the vet notes and pulling out the dates so I can spot pre-existing conditions faster. What wears me down is that I still get the medical bits wrong. Last week I paid for a dog's hip surgery that the vet notes showed started before the policy, and Owen, my supervisor, caught it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. That'd be a bit of a let-down. I'm kind of betting on it being more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that the tools are still handy, and they are. Online I'd keep it light, maybe a post about the AI thinking a hamster was a horse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be okay with the job but not totally relaxed. I live on my own, so it's just my wage, and my studio rent went up nine percent this year. Tailwise pays a monthly bonus on claims closed, and I miss it about half the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools and get better at the medical side, maybe the online veterinary terms course Owen mentioned. I'd keep the three months I've got saved and try to get to four. I'd look at whether there's a better-paid claims job at a bigger insurer in a year or so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A little uneasy about money, more than about the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the money pressure, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bonus, honestly. When I miss it, I cover the rent rise out of savings. If that keeps up all year, the three months turns into two without me doing anything wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI did a bit more of the routine work, how would that change your day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be steadier, I think. But I'd still be the person who missed the hip surgery, and that's a skills thing, not an AI thing.

Online I'd keep it light, joking the **AI thought** a hamster was a horse.
think: It's **just my wage**, and my studio rent rose nine percent.
I miss the **claims bonus** about half the time, which drains savings.
do: Take the **veterinary terms** course my supervisor mentioned.
Grow savings from **three to four months**.
Look at **bigger insurers** for better-paid claims work in a year.
feel: Fine, a little **uneasy** about money more than the job.

fieldNote: Her worry here is **rent and bonus**, not AI at all.
She already uses AI **all day** and still misses medical details.
She sees her gap as **skills**, and plans to fix it with a course.

steps.text: Take the online veterinary terms course Owen suggested
Grow her savings from three months to four
Apply to bigger insurers for claims jobs in a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, that's already happening a bit. Tailwise has a pilot where the system pays the simple ones itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be upfront about it: the simple claims are going to the machine, so everyone needs to learn the tricky ones and the tools. I'd post about how to use AI for checking vet notes, because I actually know how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the plain claims team shrinks a lot. A spaniel eats a sock, the system pays the claim in a minute. What's left is the tricky medical history, and I'm still bad at that. Being good with tools only gets me so far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer for the pilot team straight away and learn how it decides. I'd do the vet terms course this winter, properly. And I'd look at the vet practices around me, because someone needs to help them send claims to all the insurers, and I know how it works from this side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buzzing and a bit sick at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned helping vet practices. Would you really try that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I would. Vets hate the paperwork. If I could do it from home for three or four practices, I'd have a second income that isn't only Tailwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the side work doesn't take off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit that'd scare me. One wage, no partner, and if Tailwise cut the team I'd have the side work and three months' savings, that's it.

say: I'd say **simple claims** are going to the machine, so learn the tricky ones.
I'd post tips on **using AI** to check vet notes.
think: The plain **claims team shrinks** a lot.
Being good with tools only gets me so far when I'm **bad at medical** history.
do: Finish the **vet terms course** this winter.
Offer **claims paperwork help** to three or four local vet practices.
feel: **Buzzing** and a bit sick at once.
S1.quote: A spaniel eats a sock, the system pays the claim in a minute. What's left is the tricky medical history, and I'm still bad at that.
fieldNote: She jumps to **volunteer** and to build a side business, which fits her appetite for risk.
She sees clearly that **tool skill** doesn't cover her medical weakness.
Being on **one wage** keeps her anxious despite her energy.

steps.text: Join Tailwise's auto-pay pilot team this quarter
Offer claims paperwork help to local vet practices
Finish the vet terms course this winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. Okay, that's the whole job, isn't it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it calmly but straight: this is moving faster than the rules, and people need help before, not after. I'd want the government to do something, but I don't trust either side to get it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Tailwise's claims desk is basically gone by 2028, and the vet paperwork side business goes with it, because AGI does that too. What doesn't go straight away is a person holding a dog still at the vet's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to train as a vet nurse right away, it's a few years of college and placement, and I'd start while I still had the Tailwise wage. I'd cut my spending hard, move somewhere cheaper, maybe a room in a shared house. Every spare bit would go into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. It'd keep me up. But also a bit like, at least I know what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says robots for hands-on work come about three years later. Does that change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the gamble. If robots for hands-on work come three years after, I'd get maybe a few years of vet nursing before they turn up. But holding a frightened animal is hard to automate, so I'd bet on it lasting longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go back to my parents' if it came to it. I'd hate it, I'm twenty-seven. But my mum would have me, and that's the safety net I'd have.

say: I'd say it's **faster than the rules**, so help must come before.
I'd want **government action**, but I trust neither side to get it right.
think: Tailwise's claims desk is **basically gone** by 2028.
The **vet paperwork** side business goes too, since AGI does that.
do: Apply to train as a **vet nurse** while still on the Tailwise wage.
Move to a **shared house** room and cut spending hard.
Fall back on **my parents** if money runs out.
feel: **Scared** and awake at night, but clear on what to do.
S2.quote: What doesn't go straight away is a person holding a dog still at the vet's.
fieldNote: She **pivots fast** from desk to hands-on, using the three-year robot gap.
Her own **side business idea** dies in this world, and she says so.
**One income** and a short timeline make her alarmed despite having a plan.

steps.text: Apply for vet nurse training while still at Tailwise
Move into a room in a shared house to cut rent
Cut spending hard and bank every spare bit
Move back to her parents' if money runs out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's long enough to do something properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time if people start now. I'd keep posting the useful stuff about AI, because people my age should be using it to get ahead while it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd make money from the change before it finishes the job. I'd be the claims person who knows the AI best, then the side business for a couple of years, then vet nursing before AGI lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the pilot, ask for a pay rise once I'm running part of it, start the side work with vet practices in year one, and save the extra. In year two or three I'd start the vet nursing course part-time. By 2031 I'd want to be qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly. Nervous, but mostly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got three plans in a row there. Would you really stick to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. If the side work earned enough, I might be tempted to stay. But I know AGI eats that too, so I'd hold myself to the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still switch to vet nursing even if Tailwise offered you more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah. I'd just have to work out the money. Vet nurses earn less than me at first, so I'd want six months saved before I switched.

say: I'd say there's **time if people start** now.
I'd keep posting **AI tips** so people my age get ahead while it lasts.
think: I'd **make money** from the change before it finishes the job.
Tools first, then the **side business**, then vet nursing before AGI lands.
do: Start the **vet practice side work** in year one and save the extra.
Begin a **part-time vet nursing** course in year two or three.
S3.quote: I'd be the claims person who knows the AI best, then the side business for a couple of years, then vet nursing before AGI lands.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **stack three moves** and earn from each.
She knows the side business **won't last**, and keeps herself honest about it.
Vet nursing's **lower starting pay** is the cost she plans for.

steps.text: Start claims paperwork side work for vet practices in year one
Begin a part-time vet nursing course in year two
Save six months of expenses before leaving Tailwise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That feels like ages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse not to be ready. Learn the tools, learn a second thing, don't sit still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably stay in insurance a good while. I'd move into the team that sets up and checks the AI, get better paid, and buy somewhere small. I'd still want a hands-on plan for the last few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move into Tailwise's AI operations team, or a bigger insurer's, in the next couple of years. I'd save for a deposit on a one-bedroom flat. Around year six I'd start vet nursing part-time, so I'm qualified before AGI arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little uneasy because I'd be the one holding myself to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting comfy. Ten years is long enough to forget you were worried, so I'd put a date in my calendar for the vet nursing course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any plans outside work that would change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I'd like a partner one day, but I'm not planning my life around that. The flat's the thing.

say: I'd say there's **no excuse** not to be ready.
Learn the tools, **learn a second thing**, and don't sit still.
think: I'd **stay in insurance** a good while and get better paid on the AI side.
I'd still want a **hands-on plan** for the last few years.
do: Move into an **AI operations** team in the next two years.
Start **vet nursing part-time** around year six.
feel: Mostly **calm**, a little uneasy holding myself to it.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to forget you were worried, so I'd put a date in my calendar for the vet nursing course.
fieldNote: With a decade she **stays and climbs** before switching.
She sets a **calendar date** to guard against her own comfort.
A **flat of her own** is her main life goal.

steps.text: Move into an AI operations team at Tailwise or a bigger insurer
Save for a deposit on a one-bedroom flat
Start a part-time vet nursing course around year six

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd have a plan, but one wage and two years isn't much to do it with. What would help is help with training costs for people switching to hands-on jobs, and a bit of income while you're training, so I don't end up back in my old bedroom.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to be good at the new tools and still not good at the job. People assume young people are fine because we know AI. I know AI better than my supervisor, and I still miss things he catches. Owen's had twenty years at it.

headlineQuote: People assume young people are fine because we know AI. I know AI better than my supervisor, and I still miss things he catches.
portrait: Tara is a **27-year-old** pet insurance claims assistant at Tailwise who uses AI all day.
She lives **alone on one wage**, with three months saved and a rising studio rent.
She's **centre** in politics and wary of both sides getting the response right.
She plans in stages: AI pilot, a **vet paperwork side business**, then vet nursing.
She's open that **tool skill** hasn't fixed her weak grasp of medical history.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because one wage and two years leaves little room.
whatWouldHelp: **Training costs** and some income while retraining for **hands-on** jobs.
